events.title: First Iron Bridge Opens
events.blurb: A cast-iron arch bridge opened across a gorge of the Severn River in western England, the first substantial bridge anywhere in the world constructed entirely of iron. Its five parallel ribs, each cast as a single 21-metre piece, spanned 30 metres and weighed 384 tonnes. The bridge was built partly as a structural demonstration by a local ironmaster promoting the capabilities of his foundries.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1781 — Ironbridge, Shropshire. Designer Thomas Farnolls Pritchard, ironmaster Abraham Darby III. It still stands as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The surrounding gorge is considered the cradle of the Industrial Revolution.

events.title: Great Exhibition Opens
events.blurb: Queen Victoria opened a five-month international exhibition of industrial and artistic products housed in a vast prefabricated iron-and-glass structure in Hyde Park — the building nicknamed the "Crystal Palace." 14,000 exhibitors from 25 countries displayed 100,000 exhibits; six million visitors paid admission. The exhibition's organizer, Prince Albert, had intended it as both a celebration of industrial progress and a showcase for the superiority of free trade. It made a healthy profit, used to found London museums.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1851 — Prince Albert's Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. Designer Joseph Paxton, a gardener turned architect, had designed the building in a single afternoon on a sheet of blotting paper. The profit funded the Victoria and Albert, Science, and Natural History museums.

events.title: Drake Strikes Oil
events.blurb: A former railroad conductor, working on behalf of a small Pennsylvania oil-extraction company, struck oil at a depth of 21 metres while drilling a well using salt-drilling techniques borrowed from Chinese craftsmen. The well produced about 25 barrels a day — at the time, world-altering. Within two years, western Pennsylvania had hundreds of wells; within twenty, American oil companies were exporting kerosene around the world; within fifty, petroleum had overtaken coal as the premier industrial fuel.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1859 — Edwin Drake at Titusville, Pennsylvania. Drake himself died poor; he had failed to patent his drilling-pipe innovations. John D. Rockefeller entered the Cleveland refining business five years later and, with Standard Oil, came to dominate the industry within a decade.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Transistor Invented
events.blurb: Three physicists at an American industrial research laboratory demonstrated a working point-contact transistor — a tiny semiconductor device made from germanium that could amplify electrical signals without the vacuum tubes, heat, and bulk then required. Within a decade the invention had reshaped electronics; within five decades, billions of its descendants would fit on a single silicon chip smaller than a fingernail.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1947 — John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They shared the 1956 Nobel. Shockley's later semiconductor company, though commercially a failure, seeded Silicon Valley through the departure of its "Traitorous Eight" founders of Fairchild Semiconductor.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: GPS Civilian Access Improved
events.blurb: At midnight, Washington time, the U.S. Department of Defense turned off a feature called Selective Availability, which had deliberately degraded civilian GPS signals by up to 100 metres. The next morning, civilian receivers everywhere in the world suddenly had ten-times-better accuracy — 10 metres instead of 100. The change unlocked a generation of new commercial uses: in-car navigation, smartphone maps, precision agriculture, geocaching, and eventually app-dispatched taxi services.
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2000 — directed by President Bill Clinton. The signal had been degraded during the Cold War for fear of hostile actors targeting US assets. The 2007 iPhone's eventual GPS feature depended entirely on this unlock.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: Semmelweis and Handwashing
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Hungarian-born obstetrician in a Vienna maternity hospital observed that the ward staffed by medical students (who also performed autopsies) had a puerperal-fever death rate three times higher than the ward staffed by midwives. He instituted compulsory chlorinated-lime handwashing and watched the death rate drop tenfold. The medical establishment rejected his findings; he was dismissed, ridiculed, and eventually committed to an asylum, where he died of injuries from a beating by guards.
events.revealBlurb: 1847 — Ignaz Semmelweis at Vienna General Hospital. His theory was resisted because germ theory didn't yet exist; doctors took offense at being blamed for patient deaths. He died in an asylum on August 13, 1865, ironically of an infection from his beating injuries. Germ theory vindicated him a few years later.

events.title: Snow's Cholera Pump
events.blurb: A London physician, investigating a cholera outbreak in a Soho neighbourhood that had killed 127 people in three days, mapped the cases and traced their common origin to a public water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the local parish authorities to remove the pump's handle. New cases stopped almost immediately. His investigation established that cholera was a water-borne disease — against the reigning theory that it spread through "miasmas" in the air.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1854 — John Snow, Soho, London. His sketched map of the cases clustered around the pump is a founding document of epidemiology. The pump's water source had been contaminated by a nearby cesspit. A replica pump stands at the site today, with its handle symbolically removed.

events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: WHO Certifies Smallpox Eradication
events.blurb: The World Health Assembly certified the global eradication of smallpox — the only human infectious disease ever deliberately driven to extinction — following a 13-year WHO campaign using ring vaccination to contain and eliminate every remaining outbreak. The last naturally occurring case had been recorded in Somalia in 1977, ending a disease that had killed an estimated 300 million people in the 20th century alone.

events.title: New Zealand Grants Women's Suffrage
events.blurb: The governor of a British colony in the South Pacific gave royal assent to an electoral act adding "and women" to the existing definition of qualified voters, making the colony the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the national franchise. Roughly 90,000 women registered within weeks; 82 percent of them turned out for the first subsequent election.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1893 — campaigners including Kate Sheppard delivered a petition a quarter of a kilometre long with nearly 32,000 signatures. The date is now Suffrage Day in New Zealand. Sheppard appears on the country's ten-dollar note.

events.title: Girl Scouts Founded
events.blurb: A 51-year-old widow in a Georgia city, inspired by a chance meeting with the British founder of a boys' scouting movement, gathered 18 girls in her house for a first troop meeting. She promised them learning to "do something with their lives, something the world would remember them for." Within a decade the organization had 70,000 members; within a century, over three million.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1912 — Juliette "Daisy" Gordon Low in Savannah. The signature cookies came 11 years later. Daisy had been deaf in one ear from wedding-day rice thrown into it; she joked about it lifelong.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Disappears
events.blurb: On the penultimate leg of an around-the-world flight at the equator, a 39-year-old American aviator and her navigator took off from a Pacific airstrip bound for a tiny coral island 4,100 kilometres away. Her final radio messages reported low fuel and inability to locate the island. A Navy search of 400,000 square kilometres of ocean found nothing. Her disappearance has launched a hundred books and at least three feature films.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1937 — Earhart and Fred Noonan bound for Howland Island. Prevailing theories: ran out of fuel and ditched; landed on uninhabited Nikumaroro and died of thirst; captured by the Japanese. No conclusive physical evidence exists.

events.title: FDA Approves the Pill
events.blurb: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a daily oral contraceptive pill combining synthetic estrogen and progestin for sale as a birth-control product, two years after approving the same drug for menstrual disorders. Over two million American women were taking it within three years. It was the first drug ever developed for use by healthy people rather than sick ones, and it reshaped women's labour-force participation for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: May 9, 1960 — Enovid, made by G.D. Searle. The research had been funded privately by heiress Katharine McCormick because federal funding was politically impossible. Single women could be denied prescriptions until a 1972 Supreme Court ruling.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang Unifies China
events.blurb: A 38-year-old king of a northwestern Chinese state, having conquered the other six rival warring states over a decade of campaigning, declared himself "First Emperor" of a unified Chinese empire. He standardized weights, measures, currency, and written script across his new realm; built a system of roads and canals; and began construction of the infrastructure that would become the Great Wall. His dynasty collapsed within four years of his death; his successor dynasty, the Han, would last four centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 221 BCE — Qin Shi Huang (Ying Zheng). He was obsessed with immortality; some scholars believe the mercury he consumed as an "elixir" hastened his death in 210 BCE. His 8,000-figure terracotta-army tomb, excavated from 1974 on, is his most famous monument. China is named for the Qin.

events.title: Hadrian's Wall Begun
events.blurb: A Roman emperor, touring his empire's northern frontier in Britannia, ordered the construction of a 117-kilometre stone-and-turf fortification across the narrow neck of the island from coast to coast. Sixteen forts and dozens of smaller milecastles were strung along it, garrisoned by auxiliary troops from across the empire. It was less a continuous fighting wall than a filter — controlling movement, collecting customs, and projecting imperial authority. Much of it still stands; the wall defined the political frontier for three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 122 CE — Emperor Hadrian. Construction took six years and employed three legions. Hadrian himself famously declared at the start of his reign that Rome would not continue to expand its borders indefinitely — reversing his predecessor Trajan's conquests in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Dedication of Constantinople
events.blurb: Constantine ceremonially dedicated his rebuilt city on the Bosphorus — built on the site of the old Greek colony of Byzantium — as Nova Roma, "New Rome," after six years of construction. The city was positioned to control trade routes between Europe and Asia, had natural defences on three sides, and was explicitly Christian in character, with no traditional pagan temples.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 330 CE. Constantine commissioned a massive porphyry column topped with a statue of himself as Apollo-Sol to stand at the city's centre. Legends later claimed he buried holy Christian relics in its base. The column still stands in Istanbul, badly scorched but intact, called Cemberlitas.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.blurb: After Rome settled Visigothic refugees south of the Danube and then systematically starved and abused them, the Goths rose in revolt. Emperor Valens — who refused to wait for reinforcements — attacked their fortified camp with approximately 30,000 men. Gothic cavalry flanked both sides of the Roman line and trapped the legions; two-thirds of the eastern field army was destroyed and Valens himself was killed.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 378 CE. Valens's body was never found. One account says he was carried wounded to a farmhouse, which Gothic soldiers then set alight; another says he was lost in the general slaughter. Military historians sometimes call Adrianople "the ancient world's Stalingrad."

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Bannister Breaks the Four-Minute Mile
events.blurb: A 25-year-old British medical student completed a one-mile race at Oxford's Iffley Road track in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, becoming the first person to run the distance in under four minutes. His two pacemakers dropped off with 300 yards remaining, leaving him to finish the final stretch alone before collapsing at the tape.

events.title: Bannister's 4-Minute Mile
events.blurb: A 25-year-old medical student in his final year of training, racing on a windy Oxford track in a university-versus-amateur competition, ran a mile in 3 minutes and 59.4 seconds — the first human ever to break the four-minute barrier. The record stood for 46 days. His pacers, who trailed off at the halfway and three-quarter marks on a pre-arranged plan, were athletes the newspapers had not noticed. Sport doctors had warned a sub-four mile might be physiologically impossible.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1954 — Roger Bannister at Iffley Road track. Pacers: Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. John Landy of Australia broke Bannister's record 46 days later. Bannister beat him in the "Mile of the Century" race at the Vancouver Commonwealth Games in August 1954 — both running sub-four.

events.title: Munich Olympics Massacre
events.blurb: Eight armed members of a Palestinian militant group scaled the perimeter fence of an Olympic Village at a German Summer Games, broke into the Israeli team's dormitory apartments, killed two Israeli athletes on the spot, and took nine others hostage. An inept German rescue operation at the military airfield where the hostages and captors had been flown ended with all nine hostages dead along with five of the eight attackers and one German police officer. The Games were suspended for a day, then resumed; the IOC president said that "the Games must go on."
events.revealBlurb: September 5-6, 1972 — Black September. IOC president: Avery Brundage. Israel's government launched a covert years-long assassination campaign against the attack's planners, known as Operation Wrath of God and dramatized in Spielberg's Munich (2005).

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Beethoven's 9th Symphony Premieres
events.blurb: A completely deaf composer conducted the premiere of a 65-minute choral symphony in Vienna, his back turned to the audience so he could follow the orchestral score. When the work ended, a soprano soloist had to turn him around to witness the five-round standing ovation — he could hear nothing of the applause that shook the hall.

events.title: Beethoven's Ninth Premieres
events.blurb: A nearly deaf 53-year-old composer, standing on the podium while a co-conductor did the actual directing, premiered a vast hour-long symphony that broke with convention by adding four vocal soloists and a chorus to the orchestra in its final movement. The text was a Schiller poem celebrating universal brotherhood. At the end the composer had to be turned around by one of the singers to see the audience — which he otherwise could not hear — thundering applause.
events.revealBlurb: May 7, 1824 — Ludwig van Beethoven at the Theater am Kärntnertor, Vienna. He had been profoundly deaf for over a decade. The "Ode to Joy" theme is now, somewhat jarringly given the text, the official anthem of the European Union.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: Monterey Pop Festival
events.blurb: A three-day rock festival on a California coastal fairground — the first major rock festival of the decade and the template for what came later — introduced American audiences to a left-handed guitarist recently returned from London, a young Otis Redding, and Janis Joplin. The left-hander, during his set, laid his guitar on the stage, knelt over it, and set it on fire with lighter fluid. The audience had not imagined such a thing was possible.
events.revealBlurb: June 16-18, 1967 — the guitarist was Jimi Hendrix, on the closing Sunday. Monterey Pop Festival drew 200,000 people. The Mamas & the Papas had organized it; proceeds went to charity. Paul McCartney recommended Hendrix and The Who to the organizers.

events.title: Bob Marley's Exodus Released
events.blurb: A Jamaican reggae star, recovering in a London flat after being shot in an assassination attempt at his home five months earlier, released his ninth studio album. Its tracks — "Three Little Birds," "One Love," "Jamming," "Waiting in Vain," and the title track — would become the core of his international legacy. Time magazine named it the album of the century. He had fled to London for his safety; the exile shaped the record.
events.revealBlurb: June 3, 1977 — Bob Marley and the Wailers. The album was recorded at Island Studios in London. The attempted assassination on December 3, 1976 had injured him, his wife, and his manager. Marley would die of cancer at 36 in 1981.

events.title: US Transcontinental Railroad Completed
events.blurb: Officials drove a ceremonial golden spike into a rail tie at a desolate spot in Utah, joining rails built eastward from Sacramento by Chinese labourers and rails built westward from the Missouri River by Irish labourers. Travel from New York to San Francisco, previously a six-month journey by wagon or ship, now took a week. The two companies, a state-subsidized joint venture, had raced each other for six years; the route had been set by the Lincoln administration in 1862.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1869 — Promontory Summit, Utah. The joining rails were two: Central Pacific from the west, Union Pacific from the east. The spike ceremony was telegraphed to the rest of the country; the "Done" message was the first cross-country news bulletin. The Chinese workers who had done most of the hardest labour were not invited to the ceremony.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Great Pyramid of Giza Completed
events.blurb: A vast limestone monument covering 5.3 hectares and rising 146 metres — the tallest man-made structure for 3,800 years — was completed as the royal tomb of the second king of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty. It consists of 2.3 million blocks, each weighing 2.5 tonnes on average, quarried from nearby escarpments and shipped down the Nile. Some 20,000 paid labourers — not slaves, as was long assumed — built it in roughly twenty years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2560 BCE — Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops). It was originally clad in smooth white limestone, robbed mostly in medieval times for Cairo construction. Its internal geometry — chambers, passages, "air shafts" — continues to attract theorizing. It is the last surviving "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World."

events.title: Pantheon of Rome Completed
events.blurb: A Roman emperor completed a rebuilt temple, topped with an unreinforced concrete dome 43.3 metres in diameter — the largest dome in the world for over 1,300 years, and still the largest unreinforced-concrete dome ever built. A 9-metre oculus at its apex is the only source of natural light. The dome's concrete mix grew lighter toward the top (using pumice aggregate), and its coffered interior thinned as it rose, reducing weight where it mattered.
events.revealBlurb: c. 126 CE — Emperor Hadrian, rebuilding an earlier Agrippa temple destroyed by fire. It became a Catholic church in 609 CE, which is why it survived intact unlike other Roman temples. Raphael and the Italian kings Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I are buried inside.

events.title: Notre-Dame de Paris Completed
events.blurb: The main fabric of a Gothic cathedral on an island in the Seine at the heart of the French capital was finished after 182 years of construction. Its twin western towers, flying buttresses, three great rose windows, and vast nave became the template for French Gothic architecture. It survived the Wars of Religion, the French Revolution (when it was briefly rededicated to a "Cult of Reason"), Haussmann's 19th-century restorations, and two world wars — before a fire in 2019 collapsed its 19th-century spire and much of its roof.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1345 — Notre-Dame cathedral, Paris. Construction began in 1163. The 19th-century restoration was led by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc. The 2019 fire's cause was never conclusively determined; reconstruction was completed in December 2024.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.blurb: Sepoys of the East India Company's Bengal Army, enraged by rumours that their rifle cartridges had been greased with beef and pork fat, rose in mutiny at a garrison town north of Delhi, shot their British officers, and marched south to proclaim a reluctant Mughal emperor the leader of a broader uprising. The revolt spread across north and central India over the following year.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1857 — Meerut. Bahadur Shah Zafar, the 82-year-old titular Mughal, was dragged out of retirement as figurehead. The revolt's brutal suppression ended Company rule in 1858; the British Crown took direct control of India.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Babri Masjid Demolition
events.blurb: A mob of around 150,000 Hindu nationalists who had gathered for what was officially billed as a symbolic prayer ceremony at a disputed 16th-century mosque in a north Indian town overpowered the police cordon and demolished the structure with pickaxes and crowbars over six hours. Riots across the country in the following weeks killed 2,000 people, mostly Muslims. A Hindu temple now stands on the site, inaugurated 31 years later.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1992 — Ayodhya. The Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that the demolition was illegal, but awarded the site to the Hindu temple trust. The Ram Mandir was consecrated on January 22, 2024.

events.title: Narendra Modi Elected PM
events.blurb: A three-term chief minister of a western state led his party to the first single-party majority in an Indian general election in 30 years, campaigning on development, anti-corruption, and Hindu-nationalist themes after ten years of a Congress-led coalition. The ruling party was reduced to 44 seats, its worst defeat since independence. The new prime minister was sworn in at a ceremony attended by leaders from across South Asia.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 2014 — results declared; Modi sworn in May 26. The BJP won 282 of 543 seats. Modi had been denied a U.S. visa for years over the 2002 Gujarat riots; that travel ban was lifted on his election.

events.title: Article 370 Abrogated
events.blurb: The national government, in a parliamentary maneuver that took most observers by surprise, revoked the special constitutional status that had governed the country's only Muslim-majority state since its accession 72 years earlier. The state was simultaneously split into two federally administered Union Territories. Its political leadership was placed under house arrest; the internet was shut down for six months; no major protests occurred because public assembly was banned.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 2019 — the Bharatiya Janata Party's long-standing political commitment was delivered at last. The Supreme Court upheld the abrogation in December 2023. Statehood has still not been restored.

events.title: Film and Television Institute of India Founded
events.blurb: A national school for cinema craft, established on the former premises of a shuttered studio whose golden era had passed, began training directors, cinematographers, and sound engineers in a new medium that independent India wanted to shape on its own terms. Its graduates would go on to redefine the aesthetic vocabulary of both art-house and popular Indian filmmaking.
events.revealBlurb: 1960, Pune. Built inside the Prabhat Film Company compound. Satyajit Ray advised on its curriculum. Early graduates include Shyam Benegal, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Mrinal Sen, Girish Karnad — essentially the entire generation that invented Indian parallel cinema.

events.title: Zanjeer Released
events.blurb: After fifteen consecutive flops, a young actor was offered the role of an angry, incorruptible police inspector in a crime thriller that every major star of the decade — Dharmendra, Dev Anand, Rajesh Khanna — had turned down. The film's success redirected an entire industry's idea of what a Hindi film hero could look like: not romantic or comic, but furious.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1973 — written by Salim-Javed, directed by Prakash Mehra. Amitabh Bachchan was cast almost by elimination. Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar then wrote nearly every subsequent Bachchan blockbuster with him specifically in mind, insisting on his casting as a contractual condition.

events.title: Sholay Released
events.blurb: A three-hour curry Western about two small-time criminals hired by a retired policeman to hunt a ruthless dacoit opened on India's Independence Day to a tepid first week before word-of-mouth turned it into the longest-running Indian film of all time. It played uninterrupted at a single Bombay theatre for five and a half years — 286 consecutive weeks.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1975. Director Ramesh Sippy. Amjad Khan as Gabbar Singh was nearly replaced because the scriptwriter thought his voice was too thin. The original ending showed Thakur killing Gabbar with spiked shoes — the censor board forced a reshoot. "Kitne aadmi the?" became a national catchphrase.

events.title: Deewaar Released
events.blurb: A story of two brothers who grow up in identical poverty but choose radically different paths — one becomes a dock smuggler, the other a policeman — gave Indian cinema one of its defining confrontation scenes. Its dialogue was so tightly constructed that screenwriters Salim-Javed became as famous as directors, the first time a writing duo achieved superstar status in Bollywood.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1975 — directed by Yash Chopra. Amitabh Bachchan's character has "mere paas maa hai" spoken against him, not by him — the misattribution became India's most-repeated film misquote. Director's first choices were Dev Anand and Rajesh Khanna; both were unavailable.

events.title: KGF: Chapter 2 Released
events.blurb: A Kannada-language action sequel about a gold miner's violent rise and rule over an illegal mining empire released simultaneously in five languages, broke the opening-day records of every film before it in the Hindi belt, and became the first Kannada film to gross ₹1,000 crore — a moment that announced South Indian cinema's claim on the pan-India blockbuster market.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2022 — directed by Prashanth Neel. KGF Chapter 1 had been a slow-burn cult hit two years earlier; the sequel was designed from the outset as the louder, bigger answer. Yash, who plays Rocky, was a regional star of modest fame before Chapter 1; after Chapter 2 he turned down a reported 50 offers in a single week.

events.title: Rubik's Cube Global Craze
events.blurb: A 3×3 mechanical puzzle cube invented six years earlier by a Hungarian architecture professor became a global bestseller after licensed international distribution began. Over 100 million units sold in the first three years. Books of solutions appeared on bestseller lists. The puzzle's simplicity — six colours, 43 quintillion possible states, a single solved configuration — caught people who had never bought a toy in their lives. World championships began in 1982.
events.revealBlurb: 1981 — Ernő Rubik had patented the cube in 1975; it went international in 1980. The first world championship was in Budapest, June 5, 1982; the current world record for solving it is under 3.05 seconds (Max Park, June 2023). The cube remains in continuous production.

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer. The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: Top Gun Released
events.blurb: A 91-minute naval aviation film starring a 23-year-old actor as an arrogant fighter pilot attending an elite Navy flight-training school became the highest-grossing film of the year. The Pentagon had collaborated on the production, providing F-14 Tomcats, aircraft carriers, and expert technical advice in exchange for script approval and recruitment-friendly portrayals. Navy recruiting offices saw a 500 percent jump in inquiries. The soundtrack, led by "Danger Zone," hit number one.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1986 — Tony Scott directing Tom Cruise. Recruiting offices were set up in theatre lobbies showing the film. A sequel — "Top Gun: Maverick" — finally arrived in 2022 after multiple delays, grossing $1.5 billion worldwide.

events.title: Spice Girls' "Wannabe"
events.blurb: A British pop group of five young women released their debut single — a bouncy three-minute track with a rap-like opening, shot on a single take in a Lisbon hotel — hit number one in 37 countries over the following months. The five — styled "Scary," "Sporty," "Baby," "Ginger," and "Posh" — would dominate late-1990s pop culture with a "Girl Power" message that was earnest, commercial, and enormously successful. They sold 100 million records globally.
events.revealBlurb: July 8, 1996 — Spice Girls: Melanie B (Scary), Melanie C (Sporty), Emma Bunton (Baby), Geri Halliwell (Ginger), Victoria Adams (Posh). The video was shot in a single day at the Hotel Palácio in Portugal. Victoria Beckham married David Beckham in 1999; she launched a fashion career later.

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Mount Pelée Eruption
events.blurb: A volcanic mountain on a Caribbean island unleashed a pyroclastic flow — a superheated cloud of gas and ash travelling at hurricane speed — that swept down onto the colonial capital below and killed nearly every one of the town's 28,000 inhabitants in about 60 seconds. Two survivors were found: a shoemaker on the outskirts and a prisoner locked in a thick-walled dungeon.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1902 — Saint-Pierre, Martinique. The prisoner, Ludger Sylbaris, was saved by his stone cell, horribly burned but alive. He later joined Barnum & Bailey Circus as "the man who lived through Doomsday."

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Mount St. Helens Eruption
events.blurb: A Pacific Northwest volcano that had been swelling a grotesque 150-metre bulge on its north flank for two months underwent a catastrophic lateral blast triggered by an earthquake. The collapse produced the largest landslide in recorded history, flattening 600 square kilometres of forest and killing 57 people, including a stubborn innkeeper who refused to evacuate.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1980 — Washington State, USA. The innkeeper was Harry R. Truman, 83, who kept pets and a collection of bourbon at his lodge and became a folk hero for his refusal to leave. His body was never found.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Transcontinental Railroad Completed
events.blurb: Workers from the Union Pacific (building west from Nebraska) and Central Pacific (building east from California) met at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory that spring, driving a ceremonial golden spike to mark the completion of a 1,912-mile continuous rail link across the continent. The railroad cut cross-country travel from months to about a week and accelerated the mass settlement of the West at devastating cost to Native peoples.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1869 — Promontory Summit, Utah. The golden spike was immediately removed; the real spikes were iron. Chinese laborers, who built much of the Central Pacific line through the Sierra Nevada, were not invited to the ceremony. Within 25 years, four more transcontinental lines would be completed.

events.title: President Kennedy Assassinated in Dallas
events.blurb: At approximately 12:30 pm that day, President John F. Kennedy was shot in the head while riding in an open motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital at 1:00 pm. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested that afternoon; two days later, Oswald was shot and killed on live national television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby before he could stand trial.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1963 — Dallas, Texas. Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One, with a blood-spattered Jacqueline Kennedy standing beside him. The Warren Commission concluded Oswald acted alone; roughly 60% of Americans have never believed it.

events.title: Bush v. Gore Halts Florida Recount
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the manual recount of Florida's contested presidential ballots, effectively awarding the state's 25 electoral votes to Republican George W. Bush and deciding the closest presidential election since 1876. The margin in Florida's certified count was 537 votes out of nearly 6 million cast; Al Gore ultimately conceded, and Bush won the presidency 271–266 in the Electoral College.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 2000 — Washington, D.C. The per curiam opinion included the extraordinary disclaimer that the ruling "is limited to the present circumstances" and should not be treated as precedent. The butterfly ballot design in Palm Beach County alone may have cost Gore 2,000–3,000 votes to Pat Buchanan.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.blurb: A 44-year-old tribal chieftain named Temüjin, having spent two decades defeating his rivals across the eastern steppe, was acclaimed "Universal Ruler" at an assembly of chieftains beside a sacred river. Within two decades his cavalry armies would sack Beijing, overrun Persia, and reach the Adriatic, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 — at the Onon River. The title "Genghis Khan" is a western rendering; contemporary Mongol sources call him Činggis Qa'an. Genetic studies suggest roughly 16 million men alive today descend from his Y-chromosome line.

events.title: Mongol Sack of Baghdad
events.blurb: A Mongol army under a grandson of Genghis Khan besieged a Mesopotamian capital that had been the cultural and financial center of the Islamic world for five centuries. The city fell after thirteen days. The caliph was wrapped in a carpet and trampled by horses; the House of Wisdom was burned. Witnesses said the Tigris ran black for days with the ink of destroyed books, then red with the blood of their authors.
events.revealBlurb: February 10, 1258 — Hulagu Khan. Estimates of the dead range from 90,000 to over a million. The Abbasid Caliphate as a political power died with the city; Islamic civilization's center of gravity shifted permanently to Cairo and later Constantinople.

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: The Seventh Seal Released
events.blurb: A Swedish director released a 96-minute black-and-white film about a disillusioned medieval knight, returning from the Crusades to find his homeland ravaged by plague, who plays an extended chess match with a personification of Death to postpone his own. The film's signature image — the knight and Death on a beach chessboard — entered the pantheon of instantly recognizable cinema shots, as did its bleak allegorical mode.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 1957 — Ingmar Bergman, with Max von Sydow as the knight. The chess game has been parodied by Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey, the Muppets, and South Park, among dozens of others. Bergman wrote the screenplay in two weeks.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: Jurassic Park Released
events.blurb: A 46-year-old director released an adaptation of a recent Michael Crichton novel about genetically resurrected dinosaurs on a tropical-island theme park. The film's digital dinosaurs — only a few minutes of CGI, mixed with extensive full-size animatronic puppets — changed the calculus of what visual effects could do. Audiences gasped at a Tyrannosaurus rex roaring over a rain-soaked jeep; a decade of purely physical-effects films were obsolete.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1993 — Steven Spielberg. The T. rex breaking into the jeep was actually animatronic; it malfunctioned often in the Hawaii humidity. The film displaced E.T. as highest-grossing ever. Spielberg was editing "Schindler's List" at night during production.

events.title: The Matrix Released
events.blurb: Two siblings who had directed only one feature between them released a 136-minute science-fiction film in which the world turns out to be a computer simulation and humanity is harvested by machines as a power source. The film's "bullet time" effect — a camera arcing around a frozen-mid-action character while the world resumed behind it — became an instantly iconic technique. Its cyberpunk philosophy, couture, and green-tinted aesthetic defined the turn of the millennium.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1999 — Lana and Lilly Wachowski, starring Keanu Reeves. "Bullet time" was achieved with a ring of 120 still cameras. The concept of a simulated reality — the "red pill / blue pill" — has since migrated into every internet conspiracy subculture.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Monroe Doctrine Declared
events.blurb: An American president's annual address to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or political interference in the Western Hemisphere, a policy the United States could not yet militarily enforce but would cite for the next two centuries. The message was drafted largely by his Secretary of State, a future president himself.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1823 — James Monroe. The phrase "Monroe Doctrine" wasn't coined until 1850. Britain quietly backed the policy because it suited their own trade interests, and for decades the Royal Navy did most of the actual enforcing.

events.title: Caning of Senator Charles Sumner
events.blurb: Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina strode onto the Senate floor and beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts unconscious with a metal-topped gutta-percha cane, inflicting such severe head injuries that Sumner could not return to his seat for over three years. The assault came two days after Sumner delivered a blistering antislavery speech mocking Brooks's cousin; Massachusetts left Sumner's empty desk on display as a rebuke.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1856 — U.S. Senate chamber. Brooks resigned, was immediately re-elected by South Carolina, and received commemorative canes inscribed "Hit Him Again." Sumner's empty desk served as visible propaganda for the antislavery cause for three years. The incident convinced many Northerners that slavery corrupted men beyond reason.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education Ruling
events.blurb: A unanimous Supreme Court held that racially segregated public schools were inherently unequal and violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, overturning the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson doctrine of "separate but equal." The unanimous 9–0 decision, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren after months of behind-the-scenes persuasion, applied to all public schools and laid the legal foundation for desegregation across American society.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Washington, D.C. Chief Justice Warren had been appointed by Eisenhower, who privately thought the ruling a mistake. The lead attorney for the plaintiffs was Thurgood Marshall — who would later become the first Black justice on the very court he argued before.

events.title: House Impeaches President Clinton
events.blurb: The House of Representatives voted to impeach President Bill Clinton on the 19th of that month, on charges of perjury before a grand jury (228–206) and obstruction of justice (221–212) arising from his false testimony about a sexual relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton became only the second U.S. president ever to be impeached; the Senate acquitted him on both articles the following February.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1998 — U.S. Capitol. The vote occurred while U.S. warplanes were bombing Iraq (Operation Desert Fox), which the White House denied was timed to distract from the impeachment. House Speaker-designate Bob Livingston resigned that same day. Clinton's approval rating on the day of his impeachment was 73%.

events.title: Enigma Broken at Bletchley
events.blurb: A team of mathematicians and linguists working in a cluttered hut in the English countryside deployed an electromechanical machine that could test thousands of rotor settings per minute, cracking the daily-changed cipher used by an opposing military's command and logistics networks — and began reading intercepted messages within hours of their transmission.
events.revealBlurb: May 1940 — Bletchley Park's upgraded Bombe, designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, began breaking Luftwaffe "Red" traffic daily. The secret was so tightly held that some commanders were fed cover stories about lucky reconnaissance flights. The intelligence was codenamed Ultra and arguably shortened the conflict by two years.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: Battle of Crete
events.blurb: For the first time in military history, an entire island was invaded and captured primarily by paratroopers and glider-borne troops alone, dropped onto an enemy-held coastline in the face of fierce resistance. The attackers suffered such catastrophic losses on the opening day that the tactic was never repeated at this scale.
events.revealBlurb: May 20 – June 1, 1941 — Operation Mercury. German paratroopers suffered over 6,500 casualties, including roughly 3,000 killed. Hitler was so shaken he banned future mass airborne operations. The British, Australian, and New Zealand defenders were evacuated; 5,000 were left behind and taken prisoner.

events.title: Fall of Singapore
events.blurb: An island fortress considered impregnable from the sea fell in one week when attackers crossed a narrow strait at its land-facing back and advanced down a peninsula faster than anyone had thought possible. The surrender of 80,000 troops in a single capitulation stands as the largest in the history of the British Army.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1942. General Percival surrendered at 6:20 PM. Churchill called it "the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history." The great naval guns of Singapore pointed seaward and many lacked armour-piercing shells anyway — the attack had come from the wrong direction entirely.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Shrek Released
events.blurb: A computer-animated feature film from a newly spun-off American studio opened with a green ogre's retelling of classic fairy tales — sly, irreverent, and saturated with pop-culture references aimed at adults as much as children. The film grossed $484 million on an $60 million budget, won the first-ever Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, and made the singing-talking-donkey a cultural touchstone. It would spawn three sequels and establish DreamWorks Animation as a serious rival to Pixar.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 2001 — DreamWorks Animation. Directors Andrew Adamson and Vicky Jenson; voice cast Mike Myers, Eddie Murphy, Cameron Diaz. The original voice for Shrek was Chris Farley, who died in 1997; the role was recast and rewritten for Myers.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Hamilton Opens on Broadway
events.blurb: A hip-hop-based musical about the founding-era American politician Alexander Hamilton, written by a 35-year-old playwright-composer who had performed an early version at a White House poetry event in 2009, opened on Broadway after a sold-out off-Broadway run. The show's casting of non-white actors as the Founding Fathers, its rapid-fire rap-through-historical-politics, and its grand storytelling about ambition and legacy made it a generational phenomenon. Tickets sold on the secondary market for over $1,000.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 2015 — Lin-Manuel Miranda as Hamilton at the Richard Rodgers Theatre. The show won 11 Tony Awards in 2016 and a Pulitzer Prize for Drama. A professionally filmed version premiered on Disney+ on July 3, 2020 during the COVID pandemic, drawing enormous viewership.

events.title: Game of Thrones Finale
events.blurb: The final episode of an HBO fantasy series that had run eight seasons, adapting a popular unfinished novel sequence, drew 19.3 million viewers — the largest audience ever for the show. Viewer reaction to the final season's plot choices was among the most negative ever recorded for a major TV finale; 1.8 million fans signed a petition asking for a reshoot. The series had been, at its peak, the world's single most-pirated television program and a cultural obsession on multiple continents.
events.revealBlurb: May 19, 2019 — series finale, "The Iron Throne." Showrunners David Benioff and D.B. Weiss. The source novels by George R.R. Martin remained unfinished in 2024. HBO went on to produce a prequel series, "House of the Dragon" (2022-), which won back much of the audience.

events.title: First Smallpox Vaccination
events.blurb: An English country doctor inoculated a healthy eight-year-old boy with material extracted from a milkmaid's cowpox blister, then six weeks later deliberately exposed the child to smallpox. When the boy showed no symptoms, the physician had demonstrated that a mild related disease could confer immunity against a deadly one — founding the practice of vaccination.

events.title: Jenner's First Vaccination
events.blurb: A 47-year-old English country doctor in Gloucestershire inoculated an 8-year-old boy with pus scraped from the hand of a milkmaid who had contracted cowpox, a mild disease related to smallpox but harmless in humans. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with actual smallpox. The boy did not get sick. The doctor wrote up his results, which transformed public health across the world over the next two centuries.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1796 — Edward Jenner inoculated James Phipps. The word "vaccine" comes from vacca (Latin for cow). Jenner refused to patent the procedure despite the enormous potential fortune, insisting it was a gift to humanity. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only disease eliminated through vaccination.

events.title: First Ether Anesthesia Demo
events.blurb: A Boston dentist administered inhaled diethyl ether vapour to a patient in the surgical amphitheatre of Massachusetts General Hospital, rendering him unconscious while a leading surgeon removed a tumour from his neck. The patient woke pain-free. The surgeon turned to the assembled observers and said, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug." Surgical anesthesia had arrived; the previous era of surgery as fast, agonizing amputations in the patient's full consciousness was ending.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1846 — dentist William T. G. Morton and surgeon John Collins Warren at MGH, Boston. The amphitheatre, now called the "Ether Dome," is preserved as a National Historic Landmark. Morton spent the rest of his life in failed litigation trying to collect royalties on the technique.

events.title: First CT Scanner
events.blurb: A British engineer at a small electronics company introduced the first clinical computed tomography scanner, which used X-ray beams and computer reconstruction to produce cross-sectional images of the inside of a patient — the first medical imaging breakthrough since the X-ray 76 years earlier. Early scans took hours and resolved only the head; within a decade the technology could produce full-body scans in minutes.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1971 — Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI; first clinical scan at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, Wimbledon, London. Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel with Allan Cormack. EMI funded the research from its Beatles albums revenue.

events.title: HIV Identified
events.blurb: A research team at a Paris institute published a paper in the journal Science describing a new retrovirus, isolated from a lymph node of a patient with lymphadenopathy, which they believed to be the cause of AIDS. A parallel American team would publish a similar finding a year later; the credit dispute between the labs lasted years and contributed to delayed public health responses. The virus had probably crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1983 — Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier at Institut Pasteur. Robert Gallo at the US National Cancer Institute made a similar claim in 1984. The French were eventually credited as discoverers and won the 2008 Nobel. 40 million people have died of AIDS; antiretroviral therapy since 1996 has made it a manageable chronic disease.

events.title: Epic of Gilgamesh Compiled
events.blurb: Mesopotamian scribes compiled the standard version of a long cuneiform poem about a semi-legendary king of a Sumerian city, his wild-man companion, and a flood survivor they visit in search of immortality. Earlier Sumerian poems about the hero had been circulating for centuries; a single scribe, working in Akkadian, produced the integrated twelve-tablet version that survives. It is the oldest recognized work of narrative literature.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200 BCE — standard Babylonian version attributed to the scribe Sin-liqe-unninni. The poem's flood narrative preceded the one in Genesis by at least 500 years. Rediscovered in fragments in 19th-century excavations of Nineveh.

events.title: Plato's Republic
events.blurb: An Athenian philosopher completed a ten-book Socratic dialogue in which his deceased teacher argues with several interlocutors about the nature of justice and, by extension, the ideal city. The work would become the foundational text of Western political philosophy; its allegory of the cave, its philosopher-king proposal, and its ban on poets have been quoted, contested, and imitated ever since.
events.revealBlurb: c. 380 BCE — Plato. Alfred North Whitehead famously called European philosophy "a series of footnotes to Plato." The Republic was unknown in the medieval Latin West until the Renaissance; it reached Islamic and Byzantine scholars first.

events.title: Dracula Published
events.blurb: A 49-year-old Irish theatrical manager, who had spent seven years researching Eastern European folklore, vampire legends, and a medieval Romanian voivode in his spare time while running a London theatre for the period's most famous actor, published an epistolary horror novel constructed from letters, diary entries, and newspaper clippings. The book was reviewed respectably but sold modestly. Its true career began with stage and film adaptations in subsequent decades.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1897 — Bram Stoker. The historical figure he borrowed the name from, Vlad III Dracula (Vlad the Impaler), was a Wallachian prince with no known vampiric habits. F. W. Murnau's unauthorized 1922 silent film Nosferatu nearly led the Stoker estate to destroy every print.

events.title: Things Fall Apart Published
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Nigerian broadcaster published a short novel tracing the life of an Igbo wrestler and farmer in a southeastern Nigerian village and the arrival of English colonial missionaries that destroys his world. Written in English deliberately infused with Igbo idiom, the book pushed back against European literary stereotypes of African societies. It has since been translated into 50 languages and sold over 20 million copies — the most widely read book by any African author.
events.revealBlurb: 1958 — Chinua Achebe. Its title is from Yeats's poem "The Second Coming." Achebe later famously accused Joseph Conrad of racism in "Heart of Darkness." He was in a serious car crash in 1990 that left him paralyzed from the waist down; he continued writing for over two more decades.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
