events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: Donkey Kong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A carpenter named Jumpman was given the task of rescuing a kidnapped woman from a giant ape throwing barrels on a construction site. The game introduced the concept of a character who could jump, platforming levels with a beginning and an end, and a story told through gameplay. That carpenter would later be renamed Mario.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1981 — Nintendo released Donkey Kong. The name Donkey Kong was chosen to imply "stupid ape" — Miyamoto had confused "donkey" with "stupid" after consulting a dictionary.

events.title: Nintendo Famicom Launches in Japan
events.blurb: A cheap red-and-white 8-bit console hit Japanese shelves the same day as a competing machine. Within a year it had outsold every rival combined, driven fourteen manufacturers out of the market entirely, and established Nintendo as the unchallenged ruler of the Japanese gaming business.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1983 — Nintendo's Family Computer launched in Japan at ¥14,800, head-to-head with Sega's SG-1000. The NES version launched in New York in October 1985. The NES/Famicom line sold 61.91 million units worldwide.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Reaches India
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Portuguese captain, after a 10-month voyage south around the southern tip of Africa and up its eastern coast, dropped anchor at a spice port on the Malabar coast of India. He had sailed further than any previous European expedition. The local ruler was unimpressed by the trinkets he offered as tribute, but the sea route to Asian spices — breaking the Venetian and Arab overland monopoly — was now open.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1498 — Vasco da Gama at Calicut (Kozhikode), India. His expedition had left Lisbon with 170 men; 54 returned alive. He would make two more voyages and die in India in 1524 as the country's viceroy.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre
events.blurb: A coordinated series of assassinations of French Protestant leaders in the capital, authorized by the king on the advice of his Italian-born mother, expanded within hours into uncontrolled mob violence against the Protestant population. The killings spread to provincial cities over the following weeks. Death-toll estimates range from 5,000 to 30,000. The massacre marked the effective end of Huguenot political power in France for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1572 — the feast of Saint Bartholomew. Catherine de' Medici was queen mother to King Charles IX. The Protestant leader Admiral de Coligny was thrown from a window and his body mutilated. The Pope ordered a Te Deum of thanksgiving in Rome and had a commemorative medal struck.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Ratified in the aftermath of civil war, a constitutional amendment granted citizenship to "all persons born or naturalized in the United States," promised them equal protection under the laws, and guaranteed due process. Its sweeping language became, a century later, the foundation of Supreme Court rulings on school segregation, interracial marriage, abortion, and marriage equality.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1868 — citizenship via birthright. Its authors were thinking of formerly enslaved people; its practical effect reshaped virtually every area of American law. The "equal protection clause" alone has been cited in over 400 Supreme Court cases.

events.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-1 that a Louisiana law requiring "equal but separate" railroad cars for white and Black passengers did not violate the Constitution. The decision invented the "separate but equal" doctrine that underpinned legal segregation for 58 years. Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent declared the Constitution "color-blind" — a minority view for half a century.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1896. The plaintiff, Homer Plessy, was 7/8 white; he deliberately boarded a whites-only car to test the law. Harlan, a former slaveholder from Kentucky, wrote the dissent the movement would eventually vindicate.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools are "inherently unequal" and therefore unconstitutional, overturning the 58-year-old "separate but equal" doctrine. The narrow ruling on schools would expand over the next decade to strike down segregation in parks, beaches, swimming pools, and every other public facility.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Chief Justice Earl Warren assembled a 9-0 majority despite internal resistance. Enforcement took years; Arkansas governors called out the national guard to bar Black students, and some counties closed their schools entirely rather than integrate.

events.title: Malcolm X Assassinated
events.blurb: A charismatic Black Muslim minister who had broken with the Nation of Islam a year earlier was shot 21 times by three gunmen as he rose to address an audience at a Harlem ballroom. He was 39. The three men convicted of the killing included two who were demonstrably not at the scene; their convictions were overturned in 2021 after a decades-long campaign by their families and a Netflix documentary.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1965 — Audubon Ballroom, Manhattan. Malcolm had suffered an assassination attempt at his home a week earlier. His autobiography, co-written with Alex Haley and published posthumously, remains required reading in American universities.

events.title: George Floyd Murdered
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Black man was killed in a Midwestern American city when a white police officer kneeled on his neck for 9 minutes and 29 seconds while he was handcuffed face-down on the pavement. A 17-year-old bystander filmed the entire encounter on her phone. The video triggered the largest protest movement in American history — 15 to 26 million people marched across all 50 states over the following weeks.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 2020 — Minneapolis, officer Derek Chauvin. The bystander was Darnella Frazier; she received a Pulitzer Prize special citation. Chauvin was convicted of second-degree murder 11 months later and sentenced to 22 years. Protests spread to more than 60 countries.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Star Wars Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old American director released a science-fiction film mashing up elements of samurai cinema, WWII dogfight pictures, and Joseph Campbell's monomyth theory, with groundbreaking effects assembled in a repurposed warehouse with a workforce assembled from scratch. The studio had cut his budget and expected the film to flop; one executive had retitled it "The Adventures of Luke Starkiller." Lines began forming at theatres on opening morning and did not stop for years.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1977 — George Lucas. He traded his directing salary for merchandising rights; he became a billionaire. The effects company he had to build from scratch, Industrial Light & Magic, became the industry standard for decades. Campbell wept watching the film.

events.title: Pulp Fiction Released
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American director released a 154-minute crime picture with a deliberately non-linear structure, three loosely interwoven storylines, and dialogue about hamburgers, foot massages, and divine intervention. It had cost $8 million, been passed on by multiple studios, and been rescued by a new boutique distributor. It won the top prize at Cannes, grossed over $200 million, and pulled a whole generation of independent filmmakers into its wake.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1994 — Quentin Tarantino, released by Miramax. The opening Cannes screening received a 15-minute standing ovation. John Travolta's comeback, the soundtrack's surf-rock revival, and the dance scene became instant cultural touchstones.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
events.blurb: Over nine days, 338,000 soldiers trapped against the sea by encircling armoured forces were lifted off a French beach by an improvised armada of naval destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, and private pleasure craft — while a rearguard held a tightening perimeter and aircraft fought overhead to keep the sky contested.
events.revealBlurb: May 26 – June 4, 1940 — Operation Dynamo. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; they got 338,226. The "little ships" — about 700 civilian vessels ranging from lifeboats to Thames paddle steamers — became a national legend. Churchill warned Parliament not to call it a victory: "Wars are not won by evacuations."

events.title: Battle of the Coral Sea
events.blurb: Two opposing fleets manoeuvred for days without either side's surface ships ever sighting the other, their aircraft flying hundreds of miles over open ocean to find and strike carriers whose decks they could not see. One navy lost a fleet carrier and the other lost a light carrier — but the strategic consequence was that an invasion convoy turned back.
events.revealBlurb: May 4–8, 1942 — the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft. Neither fleet's ships came within sight of the other. Japan lost the light carrier Shōhō; the US lost USS Lexington. The two Japanese fleet carriers damaged at Coral Sea were then unavailable at Midway — a fact that proved decisive a month later.

events.title: Battle of Kursk
events.blurb: Two million soldiers and nearly 6,000 tanks clashed around a salient in the steppe, with the attackers driving into prepared defences twelve layers deep that had been built specifically to absorb and exhaust an armoured offensive. For the first time in the eastern conflict, a major German armoured attack was stopped before achieving a breakthrough.
events.revealBlurb: July 5 – August 23, 1943. The Germans had repeatedly delayed the offensive to wait for newer tanks, giving Soviet intelligence — fed by the British Ultra intercepts — five months to prepare. The opening day, July 5, was the single costliest day in the history of aerial warfare by aircraft lost. Germany never regained strategic initiative in the East afterward.

events.title: Rosie the Riveter Campaign
events.blurb: A deliberate government and industry campaign to recruit women into heavy industrial and weapons manufacturing work portrayed a bandana-wearing figure flexing her arm above the slogan "We Can Do It!" alongside magazine illustrations that reached millions of households, reshaping public expectations of gender and labour across a nation at industrial-scale mobilisation.
events.revealBlurb: 1942–1943. The number of women in the US workforce rose from 12 million to 20 million — a 57% increase — by 1944. Women built B-29s, welded Liberty ships, and operated cranes. The Westinghouse "We Can Do It!" poster was seen by almost no one during the war; it was rediscovered in the 1980s and became an icon of the feminist movement.

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Dome of the Rock Completed
events.blurb: An Umayyad caliph completed an octagonal Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount of a holy city, sheltering a rock Muslims believe the prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven from. Its distinctive gilded dome, 20 metres across, shimmered over the Old City; its interior walls were covered in Byzantine-style mosaics in golden, green, and blue. It is the oldest extant Islamic building and one of the earliest examples of monumental Islamic architecture.
events.revealBlurb: 691 CE — Caliph Abd al-Malik in Jerusalem. Built on the Noble Sanctuary, also the site of the ancient Jewish Second Temple. The gilded dome has been re-gilded many times; the current covering, added in 1993, used 80 kilograms of gold donated by King Hussein of Jordan.

events.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a free-standing bell tower for the cathedral complex of an Italian city-state on the Tuscan coast. By the time three of its eight stories were finished five years later, the soft alluvial ground beneath the south side was already sinking noticeably. Construction was halted for nearly a century. When work resumed, builders attempted to compensate by building upper floors taller on the low side — so the tower is actually curved. It was completed 199 years after ground-breaking.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1173 — Pisa Cathedral bell tower. The tilt is currently about 3.97 degrees after stabilization work completed in 2008. Galileo is said to have dropped balls of different weights from it to demonstrate they fall at the same rate — the story is almost certainly apocryphal.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Golden Gate Bridge Opens
events.blurb: A 2,737-metre suspension bridge painted international orange opened across a strait connecting San Francisco Bay to the Pacific Ocean. At the time the longest suspension span in the world (1,280 metres between its towers), it had been built through the Depression with labour recruited off bread lines and union halls. Workers wore (then-innovative) hard hats and safety harnesses; a net slung below the deck saved 19 men who fell, dubbed the "Halfway to Hell Club."
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1937 — engineer Joseph Strauss, architect Irving Morrow. 200,000 people walked across on opening day. The famous "international orange" color is maintained by a full-time crew of 38 painters. Bridge suicides have been an anguishing running tally; a suicide barrier was finally completed in 2024.

events.title: Turing's Computable Numbers
events.blurb: A 23-year-old British mathematician submitted a paper describing a hypothetical abstract machine — an infinite tape with a movable read/write head obeying a simple finite rule table — that could in principle compute anything a human mathematician could work out by following a procedure. The paper was intended to settle a famous open problem in formal logic; along the way it laid the mathematical groundwork for general-purpose computing.
events.revealBlurb: 1936 — Alan Turing, "On Computable Numbers." Written while he was a 23-year-old student. Turing worked with a physical analogue of the machine at Bletchley Park during WWII to break German Enigma ciphers. He was chemically castrated for homosexuality and died in 1954, probably by suicide.

events.title: Ethernet Invented
events.blurb: An engineer at a Palo Alto research lab, inspired partly by a Hawaiian university's packet-radio network, drafted a memo describing a coaxial-cable local-area network that let multiple computers share a single transmission medium by listening before sending and backing off when collisions occurred. The protocol became the physical backbone of essentially every wired office and data-center network in the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1973 — Bob Metcalfe at Xerox PARC. He later co-founded 3Com to sell Ethernet products and became one of Silicon Valley's most quotable pundits. Metcalfe's Law — that a network's value grows with the square of its users — is named for him.

events.title: Windows 95 Launch
events.blurb: A Seattle-area software company staged one of the biggest product launches in technology history — a billion-dollar worldwide marketing campaign including exclusive use of the Rolling Stones' "Start Me Up," late-night TV appearances, lighting up the Empire State Building, and midnight retail store openings with thousands queuing to buy the shrink-wrapped boxes. The product introduced the Start menu, taskbar, and long file names to mass audiences.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1995 — Microsoft Windows 95. It sold 7 million copies in the first five weeks. Jay Leno hosted the launch event. The product was legitimately a leap forward over Windows 3.1 — and a reminder that one company now effectively controlled the world's desktop computers.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: William the Conqueror Crowned
events.blurb: Ten weeks after winning a decisive battle on the south coast of England, the Norman duke who had invaded was crowned king at a Westminster abbey. During the coronation, Norman guards outside the abbey mistook acclamations for riot and set fire to nearby houses; the new king was hurriedly anointed while smoke drifted through the doors. He would never be popular with his new subjects.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1066 — Westminster Abbey. William spent the next two decades building castles, compiling the Domesday Book, and crushing rebellions. He was buried in Caen, and his tomb was opened, profaned, and emptied of bones during the French Revolution.

events.title: Saladin Retakes Jerusalem
events.blurb: A Kurdish Muslim sultan, having crushed a Crusader field army three months earlier at the Horns of Hattin, accepted the peaceful surrender of the holy city from its desperate defenders after an eight-day siege. In contrast to the bloody Frankish sack of the city 88 years earlier, he permitted ransomed Christians to leave with their possessions and freed many who could not pay. News of the fall triggered the Third Crusade.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1187 — Saladin. His reputation for chivalry, magnified by his later adversary Richard the Lionheart, made him a hero of medieval European literature despite being its opponent. Dante placed him in Limbo rather than Hell.

events.title: Joan of Arc Burned at the Stake
events.blurb: A 19-year-old French woman, captured by Burgundian allies of the English and sold to the English crown for 10,000 livres, was tried for heresy by a church court and burned to death in a market square of a Norman city. Her executioners dug through the embers to prove she had died rather than escaped. Her remains were thrown into the Seine. She was canonized by the Vatican 489 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1431 — Rouen. A retrial in 1456 cleared her of all charges. The principal heresy she had refused to recant was wearing men's clothes. She became a Catholic saint in 1920 — six years after French troops carried her image into the trenches of World War I.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Alexander's Army Crosses into Punjab
events.blurb: A Macedonian king who had already conquered Persia crossed the Hindu Kush and entered the Indus valley, accepting the submission of Taxila before meeting his most formidable Indian opponent at the Jhelum River. King Porus arrived with war elephants, cavalry, and infantry to contest the crossing. Impressed by Porus's defiance even in defeat, Alexander returned the kingdom to him — then turned back west when his exhausted army refused to march further east.
events.revealBlurb: 326 BCE — Battle of the Hydaspes (Jhelum). When Alexander asked how Porus wished to be treated, the king replied, "As a king treats another king." Alexander obliged. Within a decade, Chandragupta Maurya would sweep the remaining Macedonian garrisons from the very ground Alexander had crossed.

events.title: Rajendra Chola's Navy Crosses the Bay of Bengal
events.blurb: The Chola emperor dispatched a fleet from the Coromandel Coast that crossed the Bay of Bengal, sacked the capital of the Srivijaya empire in Sumatra, captured its king, seized cities along the Malay Peninsula, and imposed Chola trading dominance over the sea lanes between India and China. It was the largest seaborne military operation ever launched from the Indian subcontinent, covering over 3,000 kilometres of open ocean.
events.revealBlurb: 1025 CE — Rajendra Chola I, Tamil Nadu. For the next century, Tamil merchant guilds — the Manigramam and Ainnurruvar — dominated trade from the Malabar coast to present-day Singapore. This is the moment when South India owned the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Guru Arjan Dev Is Executed by Mughal Order
events.blurb: The fifth Sikh Guru, who had compiled the Adi Granth and built the Golden Temple, was arrested by the Mughal emperor on charges of blessing a rebel prince. Ordered to pay a fine of 200,000 rupees and alter his scripture's hymns, he refused both. He was then tortured over several days — made to sit on a burning iron plate while red-hot sand was poured over his body — and died in Lahore. His execution permanently changed the relationship between the Sikh Panth and Mughal power.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1606 CE — Guru Arjan Dev Ji, Lahore, Mughal Empire under Jahangir. His martyrdom led his successor, Guru Hargobind, to take up two swords — one of spiritual authority, one of temporal power — and build an armed Sikh army.

events.title: Shah Jahan Commands the Taj Mahal's Construction
events.blurb: A Mughal emperor, grief-stricken after his favourite wife died during her 14th childbirth, commissioned a mausoleum on the banks of the Yamuna at Agra. Over 20,000 workers from India, Persia, and the Ottoman Empire spent two decades shaping white marble into what many consider the world's finest building. The main dome was completed in 1648; the surrounding complex was finished five years later.
events.revealBlurb: 1632 CE — Shah Jahan. The emperor himself was later imprisoned in Agra Fort by his own son Aurangzeb, and spent his final years gazing at the Taj from a window across the river. Symmetry, in the end, was crueller than marble.

events.title: The Marathas Are Defeated at the Third Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Maratha army of 45,000 soldiers and 200,000 camp followers — including families who had brought their children on what they expected to be a triumphant northern campaign — faced an Afghan force under the Durrani king. After an eight-month standoff that left the Marathas starving, they were crushed in a single morning. Between 60,000 and 70,000 troops died in the battle; up to 40,000 prisoners were massacred the following day.
events.revealBlurb: January 14, 1761 — Ahmad Shah Durrani vs. Sadashivrao Bhau, Panipat. Fought on the same plain as two earlier world-changing battles. The Maratha defeat ended Hindu imperial ambitions and opened India to British expansion. It is said that barely a family in the Deccan was not in mourning afterward.

events.title: Marshall Plan Announced
events.blurb: At a Harvard commencement address, a U.S. Secretary of State proposed a massive economic recovery program for a continent devastated by six years of total war. Over four years, $13 billion in aid flowed to 16 western European nations, rebuilding factories, ports, and farms and tying their economies tightly to Washington.
events.revealBlurb: June 5, 1947 — George Marshall took ten minutes. The USSR and its satellites were invited to join; Stalin refused and forbade Poland and Czechoslovakia from participating. Adjusted for inflation, the plan would cost over $150 billion today.

events.title: Army-McCarthy Hearings
events.blurb: A televised congressional inquiry pit a grandstanding senator against the U.S. Army, which he had accused of harboring subversives. Over 36 days, 20 million Americans watched live as his bullying tactics eroded public sympathy. The defining moment came when a quiet Boston lawyer turned to him and asked, "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
events.revealBlurb: April 22 to June 17, 1954 — the lawyer was Joseph Welch. His line came on June 9, after McCarthy attacked a young associate. Six months later the Senate voted 67-22 to censure McCarthy. He drank himself to death within three years.

events.title: SALT I Signed
events.blurb: In the ornate Vladimir Hall of the Kremlin, the leaders of the two superpowers signed the first treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles on each side at then-current levels and restricted anti-missile defenses. Neither arsenal shrank, but the race for ever more warheads finally acquired guardrails.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1972 — Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow. The ABM Treaty signed the same day restricted each side to two (later one) missile defense sites. The US withdrew from it in 2002 under George W. Bush.

events.title: "Tear Down This Wall" Speech
events.blurb: Speaking in front of the Brandenburg Gate in a divided German city, a U.S. president issued a direct public challenge to the Soviet leader: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" The State Department had tried to cut the line from the draft four times, considering it inflammatory. The president insisted. Twenty-eight months later, the wall fell.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1987 — Reagan in West Berlin. The phrase went mostly unremarked at the time; American newspapers buried it. Its posthumous fame owes more to the actual wall's 1989 collapse than to anything it said in the moment.

events.title: Tiananmen Square Protests
events.blurb: For seven weeks, student demonstrators occupied the vast plaza at the heart of the Chinese capital, demanding democratic reforms, press freedom, and an end to official corruption. Their ranks swelled into the hundreds of thousands. Then the government declared martial law, rolled tanks into the city, and cleared the square overnight, killing hundreds or thousands of civilians in the streets around it.
events.revealBlurb: June 4, 1989 — the crackdown. The iconic image of a lone man stopping a column of tanks was taken on June 5 from a hotel balcony. His identity remains unknown. The topic is still heavily censored inside China.
